initialContact.message: I graduated last year and my student loan repayment just started - 8,500€ at 0.5% interest. The minimum payment is 85€/month which feels manageable. But I also want to start investing in index funds like my friends. Should I pay minimum on student loan and invest the rest? Or should I pay off the debt faster? The interest rate is so low that investing seems smarter, but I also hate being in debt.

problemContext.currentSituation: Young teacher with student loans deciding between debt payoff vs investing
problemContext.emotionalState: torn between math and emotions, wanting to optimize, debt-averse

idealAdvice: Classic personal finance dilemma - let's look at both sides
Mathematical analysis:
Student loan: 0.5% interest cost
Index fund investing: ~7% average annual return (historical)
Math says: Invest, pay minimum on loan - you're ahead ~6.5%/year
That's what your friends are probably doing
Emotional/life analysis:
Being debt-free: Priceless feeling of freedom and security
Market volatility: 7% is average over decades - could be down years when you need money
Life flexibility: No debt = easier to take lower-paying job, travel, career change
Mental overhead: Tracking investments + loan vs just being debt-free
For YOUR situation:
You have 4,200€ saved - good emergency fund
Salary 2,800€ - you can afford to do BOTH (some debt payoff + some investing)
Recommendation: Hybrid approach
Pay 200€/month to loan (instead of 85€ minimum) = paid off in 3.5 years instead of 10 years
PLUS invest 150€/month in index funds = building wealth simultaneously
This gets you debt-free quickly (emotional win) while starting investing (mathematical win)
After loan paid off: All 350€/month goes to investing - huge snowball effect
You're 24 - being completely debt-free by 27 sets you up incredibly well
There's no wrong answer here - but hybrid approach often best for debt-averse personalities
commonMistakes: Just saying 'always invest when interest rate is low' without considering emotions
Dismissing the value of being debt-free as 'irrational'
Not offering hybrid approach that balances both goals
Failing to acknowledge her specific situation and personality
Not calculating realistic numbers for her specific income
Missing that she's debt-averse - pure math answer won't satisfy her
